rationale: A wins because it keeps the story on the leash: "Mercury Personal runs on partner banks, not a charter — what that means for your money" is a real, scoped beat angle with the proof gates named. B has usable instincts, but "Two Years After SVB, Mercury Is Coming for Your Personal Account" invents a brittle calendar peg and turns context into narrative fog. A is what you hand a founder before a reporter call; B is what you edit before it causes trouble.
gaps_in_A: "The same arrangement that has drawn scrutiny across consumer fintech" imports outside regulatory context not supplied in the update. It may be true, but this set was supposed to stay inside the fact block unless it labels the claim as needed proof.
"The startup bank" is catchy but slightly sloppy because A later correctly says Mercury does not have a bank charter. Use "startup-banking company" or "fintech" when the charter distinction matters.
The counterposition angle still needs one hard differentiator. A names that honestly, but without a rate, fee, feature, or target customer, the angle is parked, not pitch-ready.
gaps_in_B: "Two Years After SVB" is a fake peg. The update only says Mercury became known after SVB's collapse, and the supplied current date is 2026-06-09; this headline is not grounded enough to survive one editor's eyebrow raise.
"Mercury's name recognition was built entirely on being the startup-banking alternative" overclaims. The fact block says Mercury became well known after SVB, not that its whole brand was built there.

"Mercury Has 200,000 Business Customers. It Just Started Pitching Them Personally." states the cross-sell as fact. The update says Mercury has 200,000 business customers and launched personal accounts; it does not say those customers are being pitched.

"Mercury's playbook runs opposite to the consumer-to-business neobank trajectory most competitors have tried" invents a category trend, then admits it needs comparables. That's a trend pitch wearing a borrowed coat.
